h1: How whisky ratings and scores work
title: How Whisky Ratings and Scores Work | Craft Beer School
desc: How whisky ratings work: the 100 point scale, what a 90 means, how critics and competitions score and how to use a score without being led by it.
teaser: A 92 sounds precise. Here is what sits behind a whisky score and how much weight to give it.
standfirst: Whisky scores look scientific, but each one is a trained person's judgement on a given day. Knowing how they are built helps you use them as a shortcut rather than a verdict.
sections: A score is one palate on one day

Every whisky rating starts with a person tasting a sample. However experienced, that person brings their own preferences, their own thresholds for certain aromas and the conditions of that day: what they tasted before, the temperature of the room, how many samples came first.

Good critics work hard to keep those factors steady. They taste at similar times, use the same glasses and take notes in a fixed order. Even so, a score is a judgement, not a measurement. Two respected tasters can score the same whisky ten points apart and both be honest.
How the 100 point scale actually works

Many whisky writers and magazines borrowed the 100 point scale from wine. In practice the scale rarely uses its full range. Most whiskies that get published scores land somewhere between the high 70s and the mid 90s. A score in the 60s usually means a fault or a whisky the critic thought was poor.

That compression means small differences carry a lot of meaning. On many critics' scales, 85 is a solid, well made whisky. Around 90 signals something the critic found genuinely impressive. Scores above 95 are rare and tend to be headlines. Each critic's scale has its own habits, so learn how one person scores before comparing their numbers with another's.
Tasters score nose, palate, finish and balance

Most scoring systems break a whisky into parts, even if only one number is published. A typical breakdown looks at:

  • Nose: how clean, complex and appealing the aroma is.
  • Palate: flavour, texture and balance in the mouth.
  • Finish: how long the flavour lasts and whether it stays pleasant.
  • Balance: whether the parts fit together, with no single note shouting over the others.

Faults pull scores down quickly. Sulphur, soapy or musty notes, harsh new make character or a flat, tired cask all cost points. Our guide to how whisky is made explains where many of these come from.

Spirits competitions usually use a panel of judges tasting blind, with the bottles hidden. Each judge scores independently, then the panel discusses and agrees a result. Medals are often awarded by score bands rather than ranking, so many whiskies can win gold in the same category.

That is worth remembering when a bottle shows a medal. It tells you a panel thought the whisky reached a certain standard on the day. It does not tell you it was the best in the competition. Our guide to what whisky medals mean goes into this in more detail.
Why scores and your taste may disagree

A critic who loves heavy peat may score a gentle Speyside lower than one who prefers fruit. A whisky scored 93 may simply be a style you do not enjoy. The score did not lie; it described someone else's palate.

Price and rarity can also creep in. A tasting that is not blind may be influenced, consciously or not, by the label. Blind tasting reduces that bias, which is why competitions and serious tasting panels use it. When you see a score, check whether the taster knew what they were drinking.
Using scores sensibly when you buy

Scores are a useful filter, especially in a shop with hundreds of bottles and limited budget. A few habits make them more useful:

  • Follow one or two critics whose taste you have tested against your own.
  • Read the tasting note, not only the number. The words tell you whether you will like it.
  • Treat differences of two or three points as noise.
  • Notice whether the score is for the current batch. Whiskies without an age statement can change between releases.

In India, many imported whiskies reach shelves months or years after the batch that was scored, so the note may not describe the bottle in front of you.
Check the batch before trusting a score

Indian single malts and blends now appear regularly in international reviews and competitions. That is useful for drinkers here, but read those scores with the same care as any other. A whisky scored abroad may have been a special release that never reached Indian shelves, or a batch bottled at a different strength for export.

Hot climate maturation also makes age less useful as a guide when comparing scores. A young Indian malt can show as much oak as a much older Scotch, so tasters judge it on what is in the glass rather than the number on the label. That is the right approach for any score.

Look for the bottling strength and batch in the review and match them to your bottle before trusting the number.

The best way to understand ratings is to make your own. Pour 15 ml of two whiskies into matching glasses. Score each out of 25 for nose, palate, finish and balance, then add the four numbers. Write two lines of notes for each.

A week later, taste them again without looking at your scores. If your numbers move by five or more, you have learned something important about how scores work. Calibrated, repeatable scoring is a skill that panels train for. It is learnable. Keep the pours small and the water close.
faqs: What does a 90 point whisky mean?
On most critics' scales, 90 signals a whisky the taster found genuinely impressive. Each critic uses the scale slightly differently.
They are honest judgements by experienced tasters but still subjective. Use them as a guide and read the tasting note alongside the number.
Most reputable spirits competitions taste blind, with the bottle hidden. They use a panel rather than one judge.
Why do two critics score the same whisky differently?
Each critic has their own palate, preferences and scoring habits. Differences of several points between critics are normal.
